result:
The limiting probability is most likely e^{-λ}, which none of the three solutions gives. I got this from a heuristic Poisson-limit argument, not a full proof.

**Setup.** A random [n,k] code has a systematic generator matrix [I | A], where A is a k×(n−k) matrix. The code is MDS exactly when every square submatrix of A is nonsingular. The number of square submatrices of A is Σ_j C(k,j)C(n−k,j) = C(n,k). Each corresponds to one k×k minor of the generator matrix.

**Heuristic.** Each minor vanishes with probability about 1/q. The expected number of vanishing minors is therefore about C(n,k)/q → λ. In this regime the count of vanishing minors should be asymptotically Poisson with mean λ. That gives P(MDS) → e^{-λ}.

**Solution 1.** It claims that any n−k+1 columns of a k-row matrix are dependent, so every code is MDS. This misreads the MDS condition. The correct condition is that every set of k columns is independent. The answer 1 is wrong.

**Solution 2.** It tries to rule out codewords of weight n−k, and E[N_{n−k}] ≈ C(n,k) is not the right quantity. Codewords of weight n−k+... correspond to vanishing minors, and the expected count of those is C(n,k)/q → λ, which is finite. The claim that the expectation tends to infinity comes from dropping the factor 1/q. The answer 0 is wrong.

**Solution 3.** It asserts that the limit is λ with no derivation. A probability cannot be an arbitrary λ in (0,∞), so λ is wrong.

CHOICE: NONE
